newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr steadies as bears taste doubt.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr steadies as bears taste doubt.

text.p: The Australian dollar put in its steadiest performance for a while Monday as dealers began to suspect recent bearishness over interest rates had gone too far.

The currency has shed over three cents in the last month as the market priced a February easing as a near certainty. But the economic case for a cut has not kept pace with the rumours and traders are nervous of being caught in a vicious short squeeze should the Reserve Bank stay silent this week.
"News or otherwise of rate cuts will see whether it starts to grind back to 77 cents, or whether it visits 75 cents first," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
"If rates are not cut in February, and the Fed holds off a rate hike in the U.S., a test of the high side for the AUD looks assured," said Koukoulas.
By 5.00 pm (0545 GMT) the currency had crept to US$0.7638/43 from an early US$0.7624/29 and US$0.7610/15 late Friday.

But that was still far short of the US$0.7730/35 level held this time last week and uncomfortably close to Friday's 11-month low of US$0.7595. The latter was seen as interim chart suppport with more imporant bulwarks at US$0.7550 and 75 cents.
Resistance was expected to be strong atop US$0.7660 where an old trendline support now acted as a technical ceiling.
On the crosses, it bounced to 92.75/85 yen from an early 92.27/37 and was only just short of Friday's 92.80/90.

The rally relfected the currency's persistent strength on most crosses which has kept it relatively firm in trade weighted terms. It edged up to 58.2 today from a previous 58.1 close, only a little way below its average for the fourth quarter.
This was largely due to the fact the dollar still held a hefty yield premium over the yen and most European currencies even after 150 basis points of cuts since July.
That was not true against the U.S. dollar where the last cut on December 11 brought official rates to within 75 basis points.
The futures market had gone all the way and priced in a cut here and a U.S. tightening, taking the three-month futures contracts for March to 94.35 for the A$ and 94.42 for the US$.

But doubts have begun to emerge in recent days with many analysts arguing that early signs of an economic pick up evident and the RBA would be better off waiting to see how wage pressures developed before deciding on a move.

In particular, a crucial decision on a rise in the national minimum wage was due from the Industrial Relations Commission at the end of February or early March and the RBA had repeatedly warned that granting the full claim would jeopardise inflation.
Today's data showing a surprise 1.0 percent fall in building approvals for December, coming after a 1.6 percent fall in November, seemed to support the case for an immediate cut.

But the headline data masked signs of emerging strength as approvals for private sector houses, considered the leading indicator in the housing market, jumped 7.5 percent on top of a 4.7 percent gain the month before.

Non-residential building also remained very strong with some A$3.85 billion worth approved in the December quarter, up 24 percent on the quarter, while the toal for 1996 was a whopping 57 percent higher than in 1995.
In a note on the data, Duetsche Morgan Grenfell highlighted the private sector housing rise, saying it "increased our confidence that the upswing we were looking for is in fact occuring."
That, coupled with the strength of no-residential building, was consistent with the house view that the improving growth oulook argued against another rate cut.
"It suggests the RBA is most likely to opt for the "do-nothing" alternative at the February and March board meetings," said the DMG economics group.
